rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify the limiting pairs while targeting a short run. The midpoint temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen the gradient alone to test whether the two limiting pairs respond to slope. The current last peak at 7.16 minutes leaves room to improve separation without exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The limiting pair improves strongly with a shallower gradient. Narrowing the solvent window should add separation, while the higher starting organic fraction helps keep the last peak below 10 minutes; the first peak previously eluted near 0.13 organic.

Narrow the gradient further to lift the remaining R=1.42 pair above 1.5. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset much of the added retention from the shallower slope, keeping the last peak near the 10-minute threshold.
Injection 4 achieved the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Increase temperature by 5 C to seek a shorter fully resolved run while checking whether the limiting pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

The limiting pair is strongly temperature-sensitive and may separate again after reversing elution order. Test 55 C with the gradient unchanged to assess that possibility and identify any new limiting pair, retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score benchmark.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 C to improve the new limiting pair at R=1.41, while checking that the reordered pair at R=1.74 remains resolved. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves time margin for this adjustment.

With a maximum-score method secured, test a substantially faster gradient at 60 C. The temperature-sensitive middle pair may reverse order and regain separation, though this exploratory run could introduce other limiting pairs.

Test a steeper gradient at 60 C to see whether the reordered limiting pair separates further on this side of its crossover. Changing only gradient duration provides a clean slope comparison while seeking a shorter maximum-score method.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity regime with a fast, broad gradient, since the high-temperature branch retains a difficult middle cluster. Cooling may separate those compounds in a different order, while the steep gradient should limit the last-peak time.

Return to the successful 55 C selectivity regime and lower the starting organic fraction to test whether it improves the limiting middle pair. A steeper gradient than injection 7 should shorten the run, with the lower starting fraction helping preserve early retention.

Shift the solvent window upward while keeping the slope unchanged to shorten retention and adjust selectivity. This targets the marginal R=1.48 pair, while the other middle pair at R=2.03 provides some separation margin.
Slightly reduce the slope to lift the R=1.47 pair above 1.5 while preserving the nearby pair at R=1.60. This should offer a shorter maximum-score method than injection 7.

Test a faster high-temperature method with a higher starting organic fraction to shift the difficult middle-pair selectivity. The intermediate gradient duration may preserve its neighboring separation, while this run also checks whether the early pair remains adequately retained and resolved.

Use a slope between injections 12 and 13 to seek a shorter run with both limiting pairs above R=1.5. The reduced endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so all compounds should still elute during the gradient.

At the lower starting fraction, a moderately steeper gradient may improve the R=1.48 pair from injection 11 while using the other limiting pair’s R=2.03 margin. This tests a potentially faster fully resolved method, with the endpoint still above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

With several maximum-score methods secured, test the unexplored 35 C selectivity regime for a shorter fully resolved separation. The faster gradient may balance the temperature-driven shifts in the middle cluster, though new limiting pairs are possible.

Test 50 C with a steep gradient to seek separation beyond the temperature-driven middle-pair crossover without the new bottleneck seen at 60 C. The low starting organic fraction preserves early retention while targeting a faster maximum-score method.

Shift injection 4’s solvent window upward while preserving its gradient slope to shorten the fully resolved 40 C method. This tests whether the limiting middle pair remains resolved and whether the early pair tolerates the higher starting organic fraction.

Explore whether a steeper gradient and higher starting organic fraction improve the temperature-sensitive limiting pair at 50 C. This is a speed-focused trial; retain injection 16 as the shortest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Test a modestly steeper gradient than injection 16 to locate the speed limit of the successful 55 C method. The limiting pairs respond in opposite directions to slope, so this run checks whether the R=1.59 pair can tolerate further compression while the R=1.52 pair improves.

Seek a larger resolution margin rather than further speed gains: a slightly shallower slope than injection 7 should improve its R=1.59 pair while largely preserving the R=1.72 pair. The estimated last-peak time remains below 10 minutes, with the endpoint above its expected elution fraction.

Fine-tune the slope from 0.045 to 0.0444 organic fraction per minute to balance the two limiting resolutions near 1.7. This targets a larger separation margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes and retaining the maximum CRF.

Test an intermediate speed–resolution compromise: this slope should improve the earlier limiting pair relative to injection 13 while leaving the later pair above 1.5. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes, targeting another maximum-score method with more time margin than injection 23.

Test a slope between injections 7 and 22, targeting full resolution with more separation margin than injection 7 and a shorter last-peak time than injection 22. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 16 remains the shortest demonstrated fully resolved method.
